Title: Large Language Models are Good Relational Learners
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities across various domains, yet their application to relational deep learning (RDL) remains underexplored. Existing approaches adapt LLMs by traversing relational links between entities in a database and converting the structured data into flat text documents, but this text-based serialization disregards critical relational structures, introduces redundancy, and often exceeds standard LLM context lengths. We introduce Rel-LLM, a novel architecture that employs a graph neural network (GNN) based encoder to create structured relational prompts for LLMs within a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) framework. Unlike traditional text-based serialization approaches, our method preserves the inherent relational structure of databases while enabling LLMs to effectively process and reason over complex entity relationships. Specifically, the GNN encoder extracts a local subgraph around an entity to build feature representations that contain relevant entity relationships and temporal dependencies. These representations are transformed into structured prompts using a denormalization process, effectively allowing the LLM to reason over relational structures. Through extensive experiments, we demonstrate that Rel-LLM outperforms existing methods on key RDL tasks, offering a scalable and efficient approach to integrating LLMs with structured data sources. Code is available at https://github.com/smiles724/Rel-LLM.

Title: Griffin: Towards a Graph-Centric Relational Database Foundation Model
Abstract: We introduce Griffin, the first foundation model attemptation designed specifically for Relational Databases (RDBs). Unlike previous smaller models focused on single RDB tasks, Griffin unifies the data encoder and task decoder to handle diverse tasks. Additionally, we enhance the architecture by incorporating a cross-attention module and a novel aggregator. Griffin utilizes pretraining on both single-table and RDB datasets, employing advanced encoders for categorical, numerical, and metadata features, along with innovative components such as cross-attention modules and enhanced message-passing neural networks (MPNNs) to capture the complexities of relational data. Evaluated on large-scale, heterogeneous, and temporal graphs extracted from RDBs across various domains (spanning over 150 million nodes), Griffin demonstrates superior or comparable performance to individually trained models, excels in low-data scenarios, and shows strong transferability with similarity and diversity in pretraining across new datasets and tasks, highlighting its potential as a universally applicable foundation model for RDBs. Code available at https://github.com/yanxwb/Griffin.

Title: Latent Bridges for Multi-Table Question Answering
Abstract: We introduce GRAB, a constructor-encoder-bridge pipeline for table question answering. Our method lifts relational data into an heterogeneous graph, encodes it via message passing, and transfers the signals to an LLM through a small set of query-conditioned latent tokens. This provides the LLM with a compact, task-relevant structural representation together with the flattened text. Crucially, the LLM remains strictly frozen to preserve its general reasoning capabilities; we train only the lightweight graph encoder and latent bridge (91M parameters), allowing the entire pipeline to be trained efficiently. Our pipeline significantly improves performance on relational Question Answering, with the largest gains in demanding multi-table settings, offering an efficient, principled way to connect relational deep learning with LLMs.

Title: RelPrism: A Multi-Faceted Pre-training Framework with Self-Generated Tasks for Relational Databases
Abstract: [Paraphrased abstract] RelPrism addresses self-supervised pretraining for predictive tasks on relational databases. Existing objectives often emphasize only intrinsic attributes or relational structure, whereas downstream classification and regression require different combinations and levels of detail. The framework constructs intrinsic, relational, and hybrid attributes, then clusters each perspective at several granularities to generate pools of training tasks. Pretraining across these pools aims to produce representations that adapt to varied downstream needs. Across 14 tasks on five real-world databases, the authors report a 4.15% improvement in classification ROC-AUC and a 10.75% reduction in regression MAE relative to the evaluated state-of-the-art baselines.

Title: Self-supervised Masked Graph Autoencoder via Structure-aware Curriculum
Abstract: [Paraphrased abstract] This paper introduces a curriculum for masked graph autoencoders that accounts for differences in the difficulty of reconstructing graph edges. Standard masking strategies can overlook these differences and consequently learn weaker node representations. The proposed method measures edge difficulty from graph structure and uses a self-paced scheduler to organize masking and reconstruction from easier to harder dependencies. Edges enter the reconstruction objective progressively as training proceeds. Experiments on real-world node classification and link prediction datasets show improvements over the evaluated graph self-supervised learning baselines. The work positions curriculum design as a way to improve the mask-and-reconstruct training process.

Title: When Does Self-Supervised Pretraining Help Tabular Models? A Study of Label Scarcity and Missing Data
Abstract: [Paraphrased abstract] This study evaluates masked-reconstruction pretraining across 14 tabular classification tasks with limited labels and missing features. Comparisons include training from scratch, classical predictors, and VIME, SCARF, and SubTab with a shared encoder architecture. Average improvements over training from scratch vary substantially across tasks and are not statistically significant at either 5% or 10% labeled data. Benefits appear more consistent on clean datasets than on datasets with substantial native missingness. Pretrained models also achieve higher average AUC under random and structured test-time missingness, but these differences do not survive multiple-comparison correction. The compared self-supervised objectives do not differ significantly under the matched architecture. The findings emphasize task dependence and uncertainty in the benefits of tabular pretraining.

Title: Support-Set Target Leakage in Relational Foundation Models during In-Context Learning: Model Dependence and Evaluation Reliability
Abstract: [Paraphrased abstract] This paper studies leakage when labeled support examples expose target-derived relational features that a query cannot access. The authors introduce 20 controlled leakage features and evaluate them on 13 RelBench tasks across five relational in-context learning configurations. Experiments vary feature properties and placement at zero, one, or two relational hops. Target-table leakage and the condition combining all leakage features cause the largest aggregate departures from clean evaluation. Effects depend strongly on the task and model and can reverse model comparisons despite small average changes. Integrated Gradients, mutual information, and leave-one-column-out screening are compared for detecting leakers; removing detected columns does not reliably recover clean results. A case study involving four rel-salt tasks finds related problems in native database schemas. The study identifies consistent support/query information boundaries as necessary for reliable evaluation.

Title: RT-J: Large-Scale Pretraining of Relational Transformers for Context-Efficient Predictions
Abstract: Foundation models for tables and relational databases are increasingly used for predictive tasks across various scientific and industrial domains. However, adapting existing models to unseen datasets requires tens of thousands of examples. Here we introduce RT-J, an 85M-parameter relational foundation model (RFM) that makes accurate predictions even with hundreds of in-context examples or fewer. To achieve this, we first assemble the Join, a large collection of 639 web-crawled databases with 6,023 LLM-generated forecasting tasks. We pretrain with long contexts of up to 8,192 database cells, using in-context examples from a novel lightweight random-walk retriever. Finally, we leverage context tuning and ensembling to scale up test-time compute. On in-context regression tasks from RelBench, RT-J requires 10x fewer examples on average to match strong feature engineering pipelines with LLM-agent or RDBLearn featurizers and TabICLv2 or LightGBM predictors. Overall, our work pushes the frontier for context-efficient predictions on relational data and highlights the importance of real-world semantics, context engineering and large-scale pretraining for RFMs.

Title: Curriculum Matters: Data-Efficient Relational PFN Pretraining with Synthetic Data
Abstract: [Paraphrased abstract] This study examines synthetic-data sources, curriculum ordering, and transfer from single-table training in relational prior-data fitted networks. All experiments use PluRel-generated data. Gradually increasing single-table schema complexity from 7 to 17 columns produces an average ROC-AUC of 0.703 on 23 tabular tasks using about 13,300 tables; training on the same data without the curriculum yields 0.541. A relational curriculum trained from scratch on about 5,500 databases achieves 0.638 across 19 RelBench and 4DBInfer tasks, approximately 88% of the reported RDB-PFN performance with roughly 220 times fewer relational training databases. The single-table curriculum model reaches 0.631 on the relational benchmark without relational adaptation. The findings suggest that presentation order and synthetic-data diversity can substantially affect data efficiency and that single-table pretraining already supports considerable transfer to relational prediction.

Title: Advancing Open and Reproducible Relational Learning: RelArena-α, TabPFN-Rel and RPI
Abstract: [Paraphrased abstract] Prior Labs introduces three open software components for relational prediction. RelArena-α standardizes data loading, evaluation and tuning for comparisons on RelBench v1. TabPFN-Rel applies TabPFN to features aggregated from linked tables and provides a strong benchmark baseline. The Relational Predictive Interface lets users define predictive tasks on new databases and run supported models. This early release targets researchers and practitioners, with further development guided by community collaboration.

Title: A Pre-training Framework for Relational Data with Information-theoretic Principles
Abstract: Relational databases underpin critical infrastructure across a wide range of domains, yet the design of generalizable pre-training strategies for learning from relational databases remains an open challenge due to task heterogeneity. Specifically, there exist many possible downstream tasks, as tasks are defined based on relational schema graphs, temporal dependencies, and SQL-defined label logics. An effective pre-training framework is desired to take these factors into account in order to obtain task-aware representations. By incorporating knowledge of the underlying distribution that drives label generation, downstream tasks can benefit from relevant side-channel information. To bridge this gap, we introduce Task Vector Estimation (TVE), a novel pre-training framework that constructs predictive supervisory signals via set-based aggregation over schema traversal graphs, explicitly modeling next-window relational dynamics. We formalize our approach through an information-theoretic lens, demonstrating that task-informed representations retain more relevant signals than those obtained without task priors. Extensive experiments on the RelBench benchmark show that TVE consistently outperforms traditional pre-training baselines. Our findings advocate for pre-training objectives that encode task heterogeneity and temporal structure as design principles for predictive modeling on relational databases. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/quang-truong/task-vector-estimation.
